text: Three thousand years ago, the first great poem of the Western world began not with a hero, and not with a battle, but with a single, burning word.
That word was wrath. In the original Greek, mênis — a rage so fierce it belongs to the gods.
The poem is the Iliad. Its author we call Homer. Its subject is the rage of one man, and the ruin it brought to thousands.
Here is how it opens, in Homer's own Greek: Μῆνιν ἄειδε, θεά, Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος.
In English, it asks the goddess to sing of the wrath of Achilles, the son of Peleus.
The very first word is mênin — wrath. Homer places it first, so that anger itself, and not the man, becomes the true subject of the tale.
This wrath, he tells us, sent countless brave souls down to the house of Hades, and left their bodies as carrion for the dogs and the birds.
It all began with a quarrel — between Achilles, the greatest of the Greek warriors, and Agamemnon, the proud king who led them.
Insulted, Achilles laid down his arms and withdrew from the war. And without him, the Greeks began to fall.
This is where the Iliad begins. Now read its opening lines for yourself, in Homer's own ancient Greek.
